name: 1,3-BETA-D-GLUCAN (BDG)
interpretation:
RESULT IN pg/mL REMARKS Comments
<70  Negative Indicates absence of (1-3)-β-D-Glucan in Serum suggestive of no invasive fungal infection
70 – <95  Equivocal Indicates a suspected invasive fungal infection and requires repeat testing in 10- 14 days in Serum.
>95 Positive Indicates presence of (1-3)-β-D-Glucan in Serum suggestive of presence of invasive fungal infection
>138* Positive Indicates presence of (1-3)-β-D-Glucan in Bronchoalveolar Lavage (BAL) fluid
>200**  Positive Indicates presence of (1-3)-β-D-Glucan in Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)

Indicates respective cut off values of BDG in BAL and CSF respectively.
Note

1. This assay is used for the quantitative detection of (1-3)-β-D-Glucan (BDG) in serum samples which signifies the presence of invasive fungal infection. It has got both diagnostic and prognostic application. Increasing levels inspite of anti-fungal therapy indicates poor prognosis.
2. IDSA/ESCMID guidelines recommend its usage for invasive fungal infections caused by Aspergillus spp. & Candida spp.
3. The BDG Assay combined with other fungal biomarkers including Serum Galactomannan and Serum Candida Mannan help to establish the diagnosis of invasive fungal infections before onset of signs and symptoms of infection when the antifungal therapy is most effective thereby increasing the patient survival rates.
4. The BDG assay results cannot be compared with other fungal biomarkers including Serum Galactomannan and Serum Candida Mannan as its expression in serum /BAL/CSF depends upon the stages of invasive fungal infection.
5. A single positive result should be interpreted with caution since it is associated with limited clinical sensitivity and specificity. Hence serial testing to document BDG levels should be used to monitor disease progression and response to therapy. The assay does not distinguish between the fungal organisms causing Invasive fungal infections.
6. A negative result does not rule out the diagnosis of Invasive fungal infections in high risk individuals . Such patients should be tested twice a week for early detection of the disease.
7. False-positive results maybe seen in the following conditions: recent hemodialysis; administration of fractionated blood products (eg, albumin, immunoglobulins); exposure to high amounts of glucan containing gauze or swabs during surgery; bacterial septicaemia; antitumor drugs or use of various antibiotics.
8. The sensitivity and specificity of BDG detection in patients with proven or probable IFI ranges from 67% to 90% and 66% to 86%, respectively. Also higher cut off values are seen in BAL/CSF.
9. This assay should be used in conjunction with other diagnostic procedures such as microbiological culture, histological examination of biopsy samples and radiographic evidence to diagnose Invasive fungal infections.

Comments
Invasive fungal infections (IFI) are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly among patients who are significantly immunosuppressed including hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, solid organ transplant recipients, and those with hematologic or immune deficiencies. They are mainly caused by opportunistic fungal pathogens. Prognosis depends upon timely clinical recognition and prompt administration of antifungal therapy.The techniques commonly used require invasive sample collection methods, are less sensitive and require prolonged incubation times. Due to these limitations, use of fungal biomarkers, including detection of 1, 3-Beta-D-Glucan (BDG) assay has emerged as useful adjunct test for early detection of IFI. BDG is found in the cell walls of most fungi (e.g. Candida, Aspergillus, Fusarium, Pneumocystis jirovecii). BDG is not present in Cryptococcus species, Blastomyces species,and the Mucorales (e.g.Lichthemia, Mucor, Rhizopus). Elevated serum BDG levels have been associated with the presence of a fungal infection,often prior to the development of clinical symptoms and before isolation or identification of the fungal organism viaroutine methods.
